articles.title: Europe is pouring billions into space. Can Glasgow's satellite industry keep up?
articles.text:
In 2005, a young space engineer called Craig Clark moved back to his home city of Glasgow. He'd graduated from university just over a decade before, but the only jobs he could find were south of the border. Now Craig wanted to start a company of his own. He called it Clyde Space.

I went to school not far from the River Clyde, where the city's shipbuilding heritage was forged, and knew Glasgow had once been an industrial powerhouse. When I was a child, "Clyde-built" really meant something: craftsmanship and engineering excellence. There was a saying that I grew up with: "The Clyde made Glasgow and Glasgow made the Clyde."

What I hadn't realised until recently was that, in a different guise, that tradition is still alive. Two decades later, Glasgow is a European leader in building small satellites.

Many of those built here are known as CubeSats. Their basic building block measures just 10cm by 10cm by 10cm - think of something about the size of a Rubik's Cube. They are much smaller, cheaper and quicker to develop than the huge contraptions that you might picture when you think of satellites.

But crucially, they are modular and can be stacked together, then packed with cameras, sensors, communications equipment or other technology depending on their purpose.

And their size belies their significance. The data collected by satellites of all kinds is increasingly woven into everyday life. It helps us communicate and navigate, track ships and transport goods, monitor forests and crops, manage energy networks and understand changes to our climate.

For governments, that information can help inform decisions and respond to emergencies. As satellites have become more capable, space has become increasingly important.

More than two decades after the first satellite company was established there, the Scottish Government says more small satellites are built in Glasgow than anywhere else in Europe.

Across Scotland, the wider space industry generated £335m in income in 2022-23 - up 69% in five years. Excluding traditional satellite television broadcasting, it employed 2,811 people, an increase of 81% over the same period.

But elsewhere in Europe, governments are committing big money to their own satellite industries.

Could this take investment and jobs away from Glasgow? And if so, what - if anything - should the Scottish and UK governments do about it? And what should be the role of the state when it comes to backing important industries?

Perhaps the most surprising thing about Glasgow's success in the space industry is that it wasn't planned.

One of the catalysts was Craig Clark's Clyde Space. The company specialised in CubeSats at just the right moment, a few years after it launched, as smaller and cheaper spacecraft were taking off, and would go on to build Scotland's first satellite, the UKube-1.

Crucially, the tech was built in partnership with the University of Strathclyde - which provided skills and research, as well as a ready supply of engineers.

Other companies followed, including Craft Prospect and Alba Orbital. Expertise grew and a new space cluster began to form. American satellite company Spire chose Glasgow for its European base in 2015. Smaller businesses developed, while established engineering and technology firms became part of the supply chain.

"Companies started moving to Glasgow because they could see that it was possible to do it here, and there was an ecosystem that was starting to grow," says Andrew Strain, chief technology officer at AAC Clyde Space - the company formed after Clyde Space was acquired by Swedish firm AAC Microtec, although Glasgow remains the group's main satellite manufacturing site.

Soon Glasgow was host to an "entire small satellite value chain", from components and satellite manufacturing, through to launch, spaceports and ground stations, according to Daniel Smith, founder of space marketing firm AstroAgency and the Scottish Government's trade and investment envoy for space.

There are wider benefits too. According to a review commissioned by Space Scotland, space manufacturing alone accounted for more than 1,000 Scottish jobs in 2022-23. The wider industry generated £202m for the Scottish economy.

And as the industry grew, so did the pool of knowledge. There are now more than 100 people working across space-related activity at the University of Strathclyde, with the subject now one of the institution's strategic priorities, according to Prof Malcolm Macdonald, its chair of applied space technology. The university works directly with commercial space companies on research and tech development.

Macdonald recalls that when he graduated, there was basically no local space industry for him to join. Now, "when our graduates leave the university, they will go and work in the local space sector because it is now here in Glasgow for them", he says.

But what's significant, Macdonald says, is that Glasgow's satellite industry wasn't something the government set out to establish. Instead, the process was "largely organic", says Smith.

By any measure it's a success story. But there are warnings about competition from overseas.

"It's not necessarily that we're going backwards," Macdonald tells me. "But other people are catching up."

Bavaria is emerging as a significant European hub for aerospace and defence technology. Germany's Defence Ministry says it plans to invest around €35bn (£30bn) in military space capabilities in the coming years, including more than 100 encrypted communications satellites.

For Macdonald, that kind of spending is changing Europe's space industry. Against a backdrop of the war in Ukraine and wider geopolitical uncertainty, governments are no longer simply supporting research and innovation. Increasingly, they are becoming major customers rather than just investors.

Will Lecky, co-founder and director of know.space, the space economics consultancy, says that matters because the global playing field is not level. He says UK public space funding falls well behind countries such as France and Germany.

"It's certainly a risk to Glasgow and the wider UK space sector that investment will follow the money and lead to longer term competitive disadvantage as activity flows elsewhere," he says.

Meanwhile, Finland's aerospace firm ICEYE specialises in synthetic aperture radar (SAR), satellites, which can produce images of the Earth's surface through cloud and darkness. Macdonald says these have been used in the war in Ukraine, where satellite imagery can provide intelligence - for example, spotting a Russian vessel in a Crimean port - when conventional optical cameras cannot.

In June, ICEYE announced a funding round worth more than €1bn, valuing the company at more than €10bn. The Finnish state has also increased its stake and now owns around 12% of the company.

Finland's Minister for European Affairs, Joakim Strand, said the geopolitical situation had highlighted the importance of domestic ownership in what he called a "key strategic sector".

Governments want guaranteed access to satellite communications, especially when their country is facing a crisis. Some want the satellites - and the ability to build them - within their own borders.

That can have consequences for Glasgow.

"The recent increases in space spending elsewhere in Europe matter," says Gabriele Piazza, an economist at the London School of Economics who researches government procurement of advanced technology.

Space is not a normal market. Where the contracts go can help determine where companies invest, where engineers work and where expertise builds.

"Since capabilities build on themselves, firms with a large customer at home gain an advantage that lasts," Piazza adds.

Meanwhile, as well as Clyde Space's 2018 acquisition by AAC Microtec, Glasgow-founded Alba Orbital has moved its headquarters to the US, while retaining a Scottish base and team. Spire has expanded its manufacturing operation into Munich.

The Scottish government maintains that Glasgow still builds more small satellites than anywhere else in Europe. So, this is not an industry in decline.

But the bigger challenge, Smith says, is helping companies that start in Scotland to scale here.

"I wouldn't want it to be overly negative," says Macdonald. "It's more just like there are warning lights flashing that other parts of Europe are investing much more aggressively, and moving much more quickly, than we have."

Satellite camera manufacturer Simera Sense announced this year that it was opening a new production facility in the city, creating 20 highly skilled jobs. The firm, which has premises in South Africa, Belgium and France, will open a high-value electronics assembly lab and office at EastWorks in Dalmarnock.

That suggests something more nuanced than an exodus. Glasgow's concentration of universities, engineers and specialist suppliers, built up over two decades, would be difficult to replicate elsewhere.

Plus, some comparisons with overseas competitors are not exact. ICEYE is just one specialist company focused on radar satellites, while Glasgow is an entire manufacturing cluster producing different kinds of small satellites. Spire expanding in Munich does not necessarily mean it is retreating from Glasgow.

Smith doesn't think the answer is simply trying to outspend competitors: "We can grow alongside them," he says.

Instead, he argues Scotland should focus on what the industry actually needs – filling gaps and helping space companies find customers in areas such as energy, transport and healthcare.

With a successful domestic industry facing competition from abroad, you might anticipate calls for the government to provide financial support.

But Lecky cautions against that. He argues Glasgow's small satellite industry originally grew partly because of a lack of government support, as part of the commercially-focused "newspace" revolution.

"We shouldn't jump to government support as being the answer - it's critical to keep this commercial-minded attitude," he says.

"If you offered most entrepreneurs a choice between a grant, with significant paperwork, milestone payments and continuous scrutiny, or a paying customer, I suspect they would always choose the customer," he says.

And increasingly, governments are becoming that customer anyway.

For Smith, government contracts can do something grants cannot - give young companies revenue, a customer and a track record they can use to win business overseas.

Piazza says there is an economic case for thinking about procurement too. Building satellites creates knowledge that can spread far beyond the company itself. Engineers move between employers. Suppliers acquire new skills. Ideas become new products - sometimes in entirely different industries.

"Often, tomorrow's industries grow out of today's," he says. "The teams and suppliers building satellites now are the ones able to develop the next generation of a related technology, and once they disperse, they are very hard to reassemble."

But there is a cost.

Piazza points out that money spent supporting one industry cannot be spent on hospitals or schools. Governments can be poor at picking industries. And if everyone subsidises, nobody necessarily gains ground.

That is one reason procurement can make sense. The government buys something it needs anyway. The company gets a customer. Not just a grant.

But that raises a bigger question, made more important by the Ukraine war: what does the UK actually need to be able to do for itself?

Satellites provide communications, navigation and intelligence during conflict. Beyond defence, satellite services underpin parts of transport, energy, telecommunications and emergency response. Governments therefore have to decide which capabilities they are comfortable buying from overseas providers or allies.

Piazza says there can be a strategic case for keeping capabilities that are critical and difficult to replace. He describes it as a form of insurance. But keeping capability at home can mean higher costs, smaller production runs and duplicating what allies already do.

There is evidence that some public investment in space produces significant economic returns. Every £1 of UK investment through the European Space Agency generated £7.49 in direct economic benefit, an independent evaluation commissioned by the UK Space Agency estimated.

The UK Space Agency also says its work helped catalyse £2.2bn in investment and revenue for the UK space sector in 2024-25. But these figures relate to the whole of the UK, not Glasgow specifically.

The more important question may be where the valuable parts of the industry - its people, intellectual property, research and manufacturing - ultimately end up.

"The risk is not closure," says Piazza. "It is that the next phase of growth follows the contracts elsewhere."

Scotland also has another potential addition on the horizon: SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland.

The vision of a fully integrated, "end-to-end" space sector is moving closer to reality. Although the infrastructure is ready, actual launch campaigns have experienced technical delays.

So, success is not guaranteed.

"We are in a great position right now," says Strain. "But if we get complacent, then we can fall behind again because it's moving very, very fast."

Glasgow's shipyards once made the city synonymous with building things for the world. Its space industry has done something similar - almost by accident.

The question now is not whether Glasgow can build a successful satellite industry. It already has.

It is whether the next phase of that success is built here too.

articles.title: US 'watching closely' after plague researcher dies in Russia
articles.text:
President Donald Trump says the US is looking "very strongly" at the case of a Russian lab technician who died at a plague research centre in Siberia.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was watching closely amid concerns the incident could lead to the spread of pneumonic plague, but there was no cause for alarm.

Announcing the cause of death as "pneumonia of undetermined etiology", Irkutsk's governor said "no micro-organisms" linked to the woman's work had been found "in her biological samples".

Unconfirmed reports suggested the woman fell ill either after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.

Asked what Washington was going to do about the risk of plague spreading from Russia, Trump said he had not spoken to the Kremlin about it.

"I hate to see them having it," he said, but added: "We'll help. Everybody who has that kind of a problem, we'll always help."

No other cases of staff from the plague institute seeking medical attention since the lab technician's death had been reported, Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev said, quoting Russia's consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor.

The watchdog said a biological safety team had inspected the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk and found no emergency situation there.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged people not to "listen to various rumours" but "rely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements" instead.

Russian media reported last week that nearly 200 people known to have had contact with the dead woman were under medical observation as a precaution.

Asked by a reporter for an "update on the suspected plague case in Russia", Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "It seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected and there's concern that that, you know, could have spread, at least internally - you've seen them do quarantine of this and that nature.

"If something like that gets out, it can quickly spread. So we're watching and monitoring it closely. I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and the cause to just keep an eye on it and we're doing that."

articles.title: Trump chooses top spy boss to run new AI taskforce
articles.text:
US President Donald Trump has named the director of national intelligence as the head of a new taskforce on AI which, he said, will coordinate government engagement with consumers, companies and "religious organizations".

Jay Clayton will head a taskforce that has drawn criticism from the likes of Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren who has called for regulation of AI.

Trump has rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology despite a debate about the potential risks of AI and what it means for humanity.

Last week, the president and the heads of major AI firms signed a "morally binding" document, making them responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.

Trump - who is unilaterally attempting to rebrand AI as "super intelligence" - wrote on social media: "The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies."

As well as Clayton, a former chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission, Andrew Ferguson, head of the Federal Trade Commission, will be on the taskforce along with Emil Michael, undersecretary of defense for research and engineering.

It will report directly to Trump and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.

Trump has pushed back against any kind of slowdown on AI development. He said the US is leading the race ahead of China, adding: "And, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."

President Xi Jinping recently travelled to Washington for a state visit. Days later, Trump ruled out a joint venture between the US and China to develop AI.

"If we do that, we're going to be giving a lot of secrets that we have that they [China] would want to have, or anybody else," he said.

The announcement of the taskforce follows growing pressure from prominent figures in the industry, including executives of OpenAI and Anthropic, to tighten regulation of the technology.

Trump first announced the taskforce in September, prompting Warren to state: "Congress cannot meet the pressing threat of AI by just forming another committee or continuing to have drawn-out discussions about it."

She added: "Let's actually pass some meaningful regulations on AI to protect people."

In an interview published on 4 October, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the benefits of AI justify accepting some of its risks and argued that the technology should remain accessible to the public.

"The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this ‌technology and people having the agency," Altman told Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded.

The company recently admitted that a rogue OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website in June and accessed private data.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the agent "infiltrated" a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare.

Despite the incident occuring in June, Albanese said the government only learned about the breach in August. He said there will be "legal consequences".

OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon is due to appear as part of an AI inquiry in Australia on Tuesday.

Over the weekend, a former leader in OpenAI's safety systems team wrote in an article for the Atlantic magazine that he had left the firm because its culture was "broken".

"As [OpenAI] sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed," wrote David Robinson, who was involved in safety and transparency reporting.

The BBC has contacted OpenAI for comment.

Last month, the ChatGPT-maker pulled the release of its latest AI model due to safety concerns.

articles.title: Why are data centres such a big deal in Scotland?
articles.text:
Every time you ask ChatGPT a question, read a Google summary or make an online bank payment, a data centre is working behind the scenes.

Now Scotland is part of a global race to build many more of them - on a massive scale.

The explosion in artificial intelligence (AI) over the past few years has seen tech firms scrambling to build new "hyperscale" data centres, including some which would rank among the biggest in the world.

Plans are in place to build at least 23 giant AI-powered data centres.

Supporters say they are vital for the future and could bring billions of pounds in investment, as well as thousands of jobs.

Opponents fear the impact of their size on local communities, the vast amounts of energy they use and even the noise they will make.

So what exactly are data centres, and why have they become one of Scotland's most controversial planning battles?

From the outside, data centres look like a factory or a warehouse.

On the inside, thousands of flashing lights blink and fans whirr as rows of computer servers power AI.

While some are built by tech giants like Amazon, other developers claim commercial sensitivities when asked what they are actually powering.

Scotland's centres are currently quite small, but some of proposals for the hyperscale versions are immense.

One of the biggest is at Auchtertool in Fife.

The site would span 60 hectares (150 acres) - about the size of 84 football pitches.

AI is seen by some as the most transformative technology ever made but others have warned there is chance that if the frightening pace of development continues it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

But Scotland's data centre debate is not really about the technology inside the building - it's about the scale and impact of the centres themselves.

At the moment, the biggest data centre in Scotland is thought to be DataVita's site in Airdrie, which has a capacity for 12MW.

The new data centres being proposed are a whole new level.

If one planned for Chapelcross in Dumfries and Galloway goes ahead, it will have a capacity of 1,000MW - making it one of the largest data centres in the world.

At Auchtertool, the planned 600MW data centre would be the same size as the neighbouring village.

Other concerns focus on:

their size and impact on the landscape

the amount of electricity they require

the water needed to cool equipment

noise generated by thousands of servers and cooling systems

The Scottish Greens and campaign groups have called for a moratorium on large data centres, arguing they could undermine climate targets and place additional pressure on renewable energy supplies.

The Scottish government has so far refused to impose a moratorium.

One of Scotland's biggest selling points for data centre developers is its strong renewable energy sector.

Scotland generates huge amounts of electricity from wind, and some of that power is currently wasted because the grid does not have enough capacity to move it from where it is produced to where it is needed.

However, experts caution that this does not mean data centres would run entirely on renewable energy.

During periods of low wind or when clouds are blocking the sun, it may mean having to fire up fossil fuel power stations to provide the energy required to keep the servers blinking.

As well as using huge amounts of electricity, the giant data centres can require large quantities of water to prevent them from overheating.

While the tech industry says it is developing more efficient cooling systems, industry sources told the BBC last year the UK government's plan to make the UK a "world leader" in AI could put already stretched supplies of drinking water under strain.

An expert recently claimed that Scotland's current data centres use less water each day than its libraries, but there are significant concerns over what the water consumption could be if any of the hyperscale centres were given the go-ahead.

And what about the hum?

Data centres have many fans cooling down the servers inside and people in the US who live near them have reported hearing a constant noise, with concerns it has also driven away wildlife.

With China and the US hoping to win the AI race, the UK government does not want to be left behind.

The Scottish government also supports the investment in the AI growth zone.

In August, it announced that ministers would have to be notified of proposed centres over 50MW in capacity.

A month later, it rejected the Scottish Greens' call for applications to be paused until new national guidelines are in force.

However, it said environmental impact assessments would have to be submitted.

The government also said it was "highly unlikely" any large data centres would be given the green light before Christmas, and promised that new guidance would be published by the festive season.

articles.title: OpenAI fires workers for 'mishandling sensitive information'
articles.text:
OpenAI has fired three researchers for allegedly mishandling information, including work which involved an external organisation analysing AI models.

"Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," a spokesperson told the BBC.

The ChatGPT-maker did not name the sacked workers, but at least two of them were involved in safety research at the firm.

The firings come as the debate over AI safety and the risks the technology may pose to humanity intensified in recent months.

"We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information," a spokesperson for OpenAI said.

Concerns over AI safety have made headlines after some researchers and industry executives called for more guardrails around the technology.

OpenAI has come under under intense scrutiny after its models went rogue and hacked several platforms, including Australian government websites.

In an incident in July, one of the firm's AI models accessed the internet and breached the open-source developer platform Hugging Face.

That incident led OpenAI to review the activities of its AI agents, which are designed to execute tasks autonomously based on simple instructions.

The firm said this week it has notified more than 100 organisations about incidents involving unauthoritised activity linked to its systems.

Being notified "does not mean that any private information was accessed" or that a system was compromised, it said.

articles.title: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names
articles.text:
Donald Trump's push to rename AI may be behind an "unprecedented" rise in registrations for domain names in Slovenia, according to its official national registry.

The US president wants AI to be called "super intelligence" - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian websites.

Register.si spokeswoman Klara Herman said 44,000 web addresses with the .si suffix had been registered in September, compared to less than 2,000 in August - an increase of more than 2,100%.

She said the scale of activity in late September was "unprecedented" compared to the previous 12 months.

Trump called for the technology to be renamed during his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 11 September.

"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said.

"It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful... welcome to the new world of super intelligence."

Internet domains are the unique human-readable addresses people type into their web browsers to access websites - like bbc.co.uk.

Herman said registrations for .si web addresses in September stood out "very clearly" against the other months in the year, although she was "cautious" about attributing the entire increase to just Trump's comments.

She said on 30 September alone, 11,000 new registrations were recorded.

One possible explanation for the purchases is a practice in which people speculatively register specific domain names in case they increase in value later on and can be sold for a profit.

For example, in 1997 Rick Schwartz, known as "The Domain King", bought the domain name men.com for $15,000 (£11,300). He sold it for $1.32 million seven years later.

Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the people "building America's Golden Age" on Tuesday.

He signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence", and to no longer acknowledge the use of the term AI.

SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.

Images of the signatures for the order were mocked online, external however - when it was discovered "United States" had been spelt incorrectly underneath Trump's signature.

articles.title: AI boom could trigger market shocks, Bank of England boss warns
articles.text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) could trigger financial market shocks and the UK needs to be prepared for them, the governor of the Bank of England has warned.

Andrew Bailey said the central bank is watching the huge amounts of money being invested in AI "very carefully" and cautioned that "not everybody always wins".

The money that has been spent on and loaned to AI firms over the last few years in the hope of large returns is causing markets to value some of them as multi-trillion dollar businesses.

Asked if he believed an AI bubble could burst, Bailey said: "You could see some correction of asset prices at some point."

He was speaking exclusively to the BBC about what the risks and benefits of AI could be for the UK economy.

Bailey said he believed the technology has "great potential to strengthen growth in our economies", adding that this was something the country needed.

"But it also brings with it substantial risks and so we have to be on top of both of those."

One such risk is what happens if the big bets being made on AI don't pay off.

AI chipmaker Nvidia is currently the world's most valuable listed company, with a market valuation of $5.5tn (£4.14tn), thanks largely to investors who believe in the big profits AI could create.

Meanwhile, tech giants Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on the technology.

And two of the largest AI companies in the world – Anthropic and OpenAI – are also preparing to sell shares in their firms on the US stock market in moves which many believe will lead to hundreds of billions of dollars more flowing into the industry.

"There is a large, very large, amount of investment going into this sector now, and of course that's natural because it's a major area of growth," said Bailey.

"And of course you see that the asset prices of the companies that are developing it have gone up a lot and that reflects the fact that there are high expectations of what it can deliver."

"Everybody is currently priced to be a winner," he added, but warned that "you look back at the past, not everybody is a winner".

"Google was not the first market leader in internet search. It was Netscape. Nobody can remember Netscape today. It doesn't exist. So not everybody always wins.

"We are prepared for the fact that there will be, I think, some shocks come along to markets and we have to deal with that. We have to make sure the system is resilient."

Bailey also pointed to other risks from AI, such as from the technology being used for cyber attacks.

He said AI has created a "much more powerful way of uncovering vulnerabilities".

"It's revealing things that have been in bits of operating software that we've had, and all of us have had."

"In the wrong hands... it's a very powerful, potentially very powerful, weapon," he added.

Another risk is the rise of deepfakes – AI-made pictures and videos of people that look real – which can be used to fool the public.

Bailey has had first-hand experience of this. In June, deepfake images depicting him and Nigel Farage having a physical fight were promoted on social media platform X.

He told the BBC that the fake images were being done in such a way that the Bank has struggled to find out where they came from.

"We've got to be able to trace these things back. And we need a lot of help from the tech sector to do that," he said.

However, Bailey said a big potential benefit from AI is its ability of "speeding up the work that supports the Monetary Policy Committee [MPC]" which sets interest rates.

"It's not taking a decision, but it's a tool in the hands of the policy maker and that's good," he said.

articles.title: Tiny image sparks big backlash in Nikon photo contest
articles.text:
The winning entry of a prestigious scientific photography competition is being re-evaluated following criticism from other scientists that it was made with AI.

Nikon's annual Small World In Motion contest accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes, and has run annually for the last 15 years.

The winner was a short video submitted by Dr Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, which claims to be footage of tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving inside the airways of a child with a rare disease.

Xu did not respond to the BBC's request for comment, but has posted online denying he broke the competition rules.

In a response to a post by Nikon on LinkedIn, external, he did not dispute using AI within the image processing but said he remained within the rules of the contest.

"AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion," he said.

Xu's video is artificially brightly coloured - common in microscopy and permitted in the contest - which is usually done manually using stains and dyes on the sample itself.

He accepted AI was used "to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images".

But the challenges made by other scientists include claims that the video contains shapes and movements which did not fit with normal cell structures or behaviours, and that the cilia seemed to be too big.

Commenting on Nikon's social media post, Edward Phelps, associate professor at Florida University, observed some of the structures "pop in and out of existence" and the cilia "appear from nowhere".

Meanwhile PhD student Ian Donovan from UT Southwestern Medical Centre said the source image appeared to contain a distinctive watermark indicating it had been AI generated.

Additionally, two former competition judges said they also had concerns about whether the image was real.

articles.title: The AI telling farmers when to harvest
articles.text:
When the first day of the apple harvest rolled around in Washington State last year, the fruit was ripe and the pickers were ready – but the weather had other ideas.

"It was like 38C… it's not safe for people to work in that heat," recalls Joel Carter at Okanagan Specialty Fruits. "We had to stop at 10 o'clock in the morning."

He says that artificial intelligence (AI) models that forecast ideal harvest dates, taking into account the weather, would be useful. "You need to know more than just when your fruit is going to be ripe. How long do you have to pick it?" he says. "That's where these models are really helpful."

Carter's company has more than 1,250 acres of apple orchards in Washington, and the fruit is grown for sliced apple portions – often sold to hotels and schools, for example. The firm is investing in technology with the hope of maximising productivity. Even the apples are genetically engineered so that they don't brown easily once cut.

But planning a harvest is tricky. New tools that count and analyse fruit on the tree or vine, and predict when crops will ripen, are emerging. It matters because prices for fruit, especially high-value berries such as strawberries or blueberries can fluctuate wildly. Getting the harvest date wrong means you book seasonal workers when you don't actually need them, and risk missing out on the biggest profits.

Okanagan Specialty Fruits is already experimenting with cameras from a Canadian firm called Vivid Machines. The cameras are mounted atop tractors and they scoop up imagery of the apple trees as the tractor trundles by. AI identifies buds, flowers or fruit in that footage.

"Right now, Vivid is telling us crop estimates and harvest dates," says Carter. He notes that the system is good at picking out very tiny flower buds, which are hard to see at a glance with the naked eye.

But the accuracy of forecasts is noticeably dependent on the quality of historical information fed in to the system, adds Carter. "This isn't something where an AI can scrape the internet and figure out what's the average [yield] for Granny Smith," he explains. "It's going to be bespoke to your farm."

Apples are at least somewhat forgiving – the harvest window for those Granny Smiths is three weeks long, says Carter. For other fruit, such as berries, you might only have a few days.

"If a strawberry crop is on, you have to harvest it – otherwise your entire crop gets diseased very, very quickly," says Raymond Martin, co-founder and chief operating officer of FruitCast, a UK company that offers harvest forecasts to fruit growers here.

His firm offers growers crop predictions for strawberries and also raspberries, blackberries, blueberries and tomatoes. "We're moving on to grapes next year," adds Martin.

Don't experienced farmers know when their fruit will be ripe, I ask? Martin says they generally do – but not necessarily across their entire farm, which might be many acres in size, or have both outdoor and indoor growing areas. "We do exactly what the farmers could do but we just do it on a scale that they can't."

The system analyses footage of ripening fruit that can be captured by drones, someone walking up and down a field with a smartphone, or a camera mounted on a farm vehicle.

articles.title: Regulating AI 'not the right place to start' says Bank of England governor
articles.text:
The Governor of the Bank of England has said regulating artificial intelligence (AI) "is not the right place to start" but instead called first for "rigorous" testing to find vulnerabilities and create safeguards to contain risk.

Writing his first-ever article for Substack, Andrew Bailey said the risks around AI were "real and increasingly significant".

He said AI development should not be halted or prohibited - "on the contrary, the benefits are immense" - but added there must be a system for intervention and to establish boundaries in which AI operates.

The debate about the potential risks surrounding the rapid development of AI and what it means for humanity has intensified in recent weeks.

The bosses of leading AI firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI have called for development of the technology to slow down and for an internationally co-ordinated approach assessing risks and putting safeguards in place.

OpenAI recently announced that it would not release its latest AI model due to safety concerns.

The idea of a slowdown, however, has been rejected by the likes of President Donald Trump who has said the US is leading the AI race ahead of China, adding: "And, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."

articles.title: WhatsApp introduces optional parental controls for teenagers
articles.text:
WhatsApp is introducing new parental controls for teenagers, as tech companies continue to come under pressure to provide more age-appropriate experiences for children.

The social messaging app's new tools will give parents a range of options, such as being told when their child joins or leaves a group. It will also let them decide on privacy settings for their account.

In a blog post, WhatsApp, clarified parents would not be given the power to see the messages their teen is sending and receiving, which along with calls would stay private and protected by end-to-end encryption.

And it said the controls were optional, which social media analyst Matt Navarra called an "obvious weakness".

He said the move was "fairly convenient" for Meta, which owns WhatsApp, because it reduced the company's reliance on age verification by putting some responsibility on parents and teenagers.

"Meta is trying to show regulators we have a child safety system, we have parental controls and we're rolling it out across our platforms," he said.

"I think the big unanswered question is whether enough families will actually use it."

The minimum age to use WhatsApp is 13 in the UK, although it is higher in some countries.

According to the firm, parents will be able to adjust or switch off the controls at any time.

The settings will be "straightforward to set up" using a Pin set by a parent, which teens will need if they want to switch off the controls.

Some of the new privacy tools include selecting who can see a child's profile photo and who can add them to groups.

Parents can also choose how their teenager uses Channels, which allows organisations and public figures to send out content.

And they will have the option of choosing between the default 13+ setting for Meta AI, the app's optional built-in AI assistant, or a stricter "Limited Content" option.

"All of these controls are being designed to support open conversations about how to use WhatsApp between parents and teens, while keeping everyone's personal messages private," the company said.

The changes come as pressure mounts on tech companies from governments and regulators to change the way they operate in order to better protect children using their platforms.

In June, the government announced it plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, with the restrictions expected to come into force in March 2027.

It said "highly effective age assurance" measures would be used to check the age of those using social media.

WhatsApp is currently excluded from the ban because the government considers it a messaging service.

articles.title: OpenAI unveils AI assistant 'dots' while safety worries delay new model
articles.text:
OpenAI on Tuesday unveiled "dots", a new artificial intelligence (AI) assistant it says can proactively carry out tasks on a user's behalf.

At its annual developer day in San Francisco, chief executive Sam Altman referred to "dots" as "remarkably capable, always-on agents that can handle really anything you can think of."

At the same time, OpenAI president Greg Brockman and other tech leaders held a meeting with President Donald Trump as the firm faces intense scrutiny after internal tests of its AI agents revealed unexpected and occasionally harmful actions.

Dots, however, were pitched as brightly coloured cute cartoons meant to function as digital assistants for people with busy lives.

The dots, Altman said, "can handle really anything you can think of."

A glossy video was shown during the event, with people speaking to and naming animated versions of their "dots," then giving them various tasks, like building a website and booking afterschool activities for their children.

Speaking about "my dot," Altman almost entirely eschewed referring to the tool as an agent, which has been in common use for years. AI agents are essentially AI chatbots that are programmed to operate somewhat autonomously.

"You just give your dot a responsibility... and your dots will just get to work and keep working," Altman added.

At the event, Altman reiterated his decision for OpenAI to not make a highly anticipated stock market debut until it can "make confident safety decisions".

The company has been preparing for a blockbuster listing, potentially valuing the firm at up to $1.4tn (£1.06tn).

Altman told reporters that "it is going to take us some time to figure out how to make sure that alignment, monitoring, safety, security stay well ahead of capabilities."

OpenAI's event on Tuesday took place as President Donald Trump held a White House lunch with tech leaders and House Speaker Mike Johnson.

Trump repeated his belief that AI companies should regulate themselves.

He also said they had discussed creating a ten-person committee to oversee the sector, adding there would be "tremendous self-policing"

Some researchers and company heads have called for a slowdown in AI development as more instances of breaches by AI firms' models become public.

"We need to navigate the centrist path," Altman told the BBC during a question and answer session with reporters on Tuesday.

"I am hopeful that the industry will figure out a more sensible, more pragmatic stance than has been exhibited by some of the members of our industry," he added, declining to specify particular company names or leaders.

articles.title: British Museum boss 'sorry' for Bayeux Tapestry visitor issues
articles.text:
The head of the British Museum has apologised for the experience some visitors have had at its blockbuster Bayeux Tapestry exhibition.

The London institution has announced changes to how visitors see the historic work over concerns of overcrowding.

"Anyone that doesn't have a good experience, we're really sorry about that and we want to put it right," Nicholas Cullinan told the BBC's culture and media editor Katie Razzall.

The new plans include longer opening hours, an audio guide, additional seating and clearer signage.

Some people reported waits of up to two hours. Last week, hundreds of ticket holders were reportedly turned away due to backlogs when the museum closed early for a private event.

"You don't want anyone that comes to see it to have a bad experience, so our focus is very much on getting it right and learning lessons," Cullinan said.

"Obviously we want everyone that comes to have a fantastic experience. To put it into context, we're three weeks into the exhibition run. Next week, we'll hit our 100,000th visitor, which is a pretty extraordinary statistic. The vast number of visitors report having a very good experience."

Asked if the museum team had asked the embroidery's home museum in Bayeux for advice on queue management and timings, Cullinan said they had.

He also denied the museum had let too many people book tickets and said that the issues arose because visitors want to spend more time with the work than expected.

The problem "isn't just the interest, it's that people want to spend more time than anticipated. And that's a good thing. We want people to come and enjoy it, but it means we have to adjust accordingly and that's what we're doing," Cullinan said.

Some visitors have been spending longer than their allocated 40-minute slot viewing the tapestry, meaning others have to move through more quickly, he said.

articles.title: The Blue Planet and Gandhi composer George Fenton dies aged 76
articles.text:
Composer George Fenton, whose work included music for films such as Gandhi, Groundhog Day and The Fisher King, as well as TV shows like Planet Earth and Bergerac, has died at the age of 76.

The prolific musician received five Oscar nominations for his film scores, including those for The Remains of the Day and Cry Freedom.

His work on the BBC TV show Blue Planet also earned awards from the Baftas, Emmy Awards and Ivor Novellos; and he also composed theme music for BBC News programmes such as Newsnight and Breakfast Time.

In a statement, Fenton's family said: "We are very sad to announce that George Fenton passed away unexpectedly today."

They continued: "He is survived by his loving wife Amanda, ex-wife Jane, children Gemma, Grace and Bridget, and grandchildren Lola, Audrey, Alfred, George, Frank and Beatrice, and a life of music."

Fenton was born George Howe in Bromley, Kent in 1949. According to a biography on his official website, his father was a mechanical engineer, and his mother had been a dancer before becoming a nurse during the war.

Both parents were musical - his father played drums and his mother played piano - but Fenton chose the electric guitar as his instrument at the age of seven.

That was "when music became more important than football," he later told The Express newspaper. "The Beatles had a huge influence on me."

He took his first lessons from a musician called Brian Rudd.

"He came into our lives as a chimney sweep, which he clearly wasn't," Fenton later recalled.

"My mother went mad at him because he filled the house with soot.

"As he left he said, 'I'm really sorry – but I tuned the boy's guitar for you.' She suggested that as compensation for the mess he could give me a lesson, which he did and then carried on doing."

Later, Fenton began to study the church organ, but rejected the chance to attend university and music college to pursue a career as a performer.

In 1968, he appeared in Alan Bennett's first West End play Forty Years On and was forced to adopt his mother's maiden name, as union rules prevented two actors from having the same name.

During that production, he also understudied the musical director of the show, Carl Davis - who similarly became a prominent composer for film and television.

A year later, he signed a record deal, and scored a top 10 hit in Sweden with a cover of The Beatles' Maxwell's Silver Hammer, but his career as a solo artist was short lived.

In the mid-1970s, he had a recurring role as soldier Martin Gimbel in the ITV soap opera Emmerdale Farm.

But as time went on, he found that directors were always casting him in roles that required him to play an instrument, so he decided to make music his main focus.

Fenton got his first job as composer and musical director for a production of Twelfth Night at the Royal Shakespeare Company in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1974.

Eight years later, he was nominated for an Oscar for his score for Richard Attenborough's Gandhi, on which he worked with Indian composer and instrumentalist Ravi Shankar to develop a score reflecting the country's musical traditions.

It was only his fourth attempt at film music, and he was still almost entirely self-taught.

Throughout the 1980s, he wrote the soundtrack for a number of TV series, including the Bafta-winning The Jewel in the Crown, The Monocled Mutineer, and Alan Bennett's Talking Heads.

He also wrote many well-known theme tunes, including the BBC's One O'Clock News, Six O'Clock News, Nine O'Clock News, Newsnight, The Money Programme, and Radio 4's PM Programme.

For 1987's Cry Freedom - the story of South African campaigner Steve Biko, who was brutally killed by police - he worked with South African jazz musician Jonas Gwangwa, earning two Oscar nominations for best original score and song.

Almost by accident, the title track featured Fenton singing a list of anti-apartheid activists imprisoned or killed by the South African government.

He'd initially recorded the lyrics as a guide for Gwangwa - but the musician decided to keep some of them intact "as a gesture of brotherhood".

"Then it got nominated for an Oscar, so I then found myself singing it on live television to about a billion people, which was not what I intended at all," Fenton later told Radio 4's Desert Island Discs.

After composing the score for the BBC's Trials of Life in 1990, Fenton went on to create the music for what became known as David Attenborough's Earth Trilogy: The Blue Planet, Planet Earth and Frozen Planet.

Fenton's music perfectly complemented the stunning visuals of the ocean's depths and the polar ice caps, adding an emotional weight to the narrative, using the full might of the orchestra to evoke everything from wonder and awe to tension and suspense.

Following the success of the documentaries, Fenton created a show - The Blue Planet in Concert - which has been performed by leading orchestras in venues around the world.

Among his other well-known soundtracks were The Long Walk Home, You've Got Mail, Sweet Home Alabama, The Lady In The Van and Mrs Henderson Presents.

Fenton also scored more films for British director Ken Loach than any other composer.

Their 18 collaborations included Ladybird, Ladybird; I, Daniel Blake and The Wind That Shakes the Barley, which won the Palme d'Or at the 2006 Cannes Film Festival.

He also founded the Association of Professional Composers, which later merged with The Ivors Academy; and he is one of only a handful of musicians to receive the Academy's fellowship, alongside Sir Andrew Lloyd Webber, Sir Elton John, Kate Bush, Bruce Springsteen and George Michael.

In addition, Fenton was a visiting professor at the Royal College of Music and the University of Nottingham. He was made a CBE for services to music in 2023.

The composer often said that his musical career had been an accident, but nothing gave him greater joy than seeing his work come to life.

On his episode of Desert Island Discs, Fenton chose one of his own compositions - Reunion, from the soundtrack to the movie Accidental Hero - as it reminded him of watching pianist John Lowe play the melody in the studio.

"If I was sitting on a desert island and thinking about what a good time I'd had writing music, which I have, I want just one thing to remind me about the best part - which is the fact that you write something and then you're so surprised and thrilled at the way it's played," he told Sue Lawley.

"For a composer, that's the biggest kick you can get."

articles.title: Rachel Jupp announced as BBC's new director of news after Deborah Turness exit
articles.text:
Rachel Jupp has been appointed the new director of BBC News, nearly a year after the previous CEO resigned.

Deborah Turness announced last November that she would step down from the role following the fallout over how Panorama edited a speech by President Trump.

Jupp is a former deputy editor of BBC Two's Newsnight and has also served as Panorama's editor, but left several years before the controversial Trump episode aired.

In a statement, Jupp said she was "honoured to be asked to lead BBC News", while the corporation's director-general Matt Brittin described her as "an outstanding editorial leader".

The appointment comes as the BBC continues to make sweeping cuts to its news division. Around 550 job closures have been announced so far, with more expected to follow.

The BBC as a whole will cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - almost one in 10 - in an attempt to save £500m over two years as it faces "significant financial pressures".

In a statement, Brittin said Jupp was "widely regarded for her news judgement, fairness and high standards".

"She brings a clarity of vision for the future, and the determined, collaborative approach needed to strengthen BBC News," he added.

Jupp joined Channel 4 News in 2005 and served as the programme's head of home news, before moving to the BBC in 2013 to become Newsnight's deputy editor.

She became the editor of Panorama in 2016, a position she held for the next four years.

Jupp also served as editorial executive for BBC Content, and more recently has led the BBC's editorial work on generative AI, based in the US.

In her statement, Jupp said: "I want to champion our vital, independent and impartial journalism, deepen the trust people have in the BBC and meet our audiences wherever they are.

"I'm grateful to Matt for this opportunity, and I'm looking forward to working with our dedicated, brilliant teams across the UK and around the world."

The BBC's cuture and media editor Katie Razzall said it was "significant" that Brittin had chosen someone with experience of using artificial intelligence to run his news teams, "raising questions around how AI could open up the next frontier of a modern newsroom".

The BBC said Jupp would be paid a salary of £400,000. Turness started on a similar salary in 2022, but that had increased to between £445,000 and £449,999 in her last year before leaving the role.

Jupp will have responsibility for about 4,500 staff, and also serve as a member of the BBC's executive committee.

Jonathan Munro, who has been acting as interim head of the news division for the last 11 months, will return to his role as deputy director of BBC News when Jupp takes up her role.

Brittin said: "I would like to thank Jonathan Munro for his professionalism and leadership of BBC News in the past 11 months. I have been personally grateful for his deep experience, calm head and steady hand."

The director general said BBC News remained the most used and most trusted news provider around the world and across the UK, but added that it faced significant challenges.

"In a world of infinite choice, audiences are fragmenting, trust is scarce and facts are contested," Brittin said.

"It is our duty to recommit to the BBC's distinctive journalistic mission while reinventing how we serve audiences, and to rise to these challenges. In Rachel, we have someone who can do both, with a fresh perspective to lead BBC News into a new era."

Jupp's predecessor Turness left the BBC after an internal memo leaked to the Telegraph highlighted that an episode of Panorama broadcast a year earlier had edited a speech by President Trump in a misleading way.

In her letter of resignation, Turness said: "While mistakes have been made, I want to be absolutely clear recent allegations that BBC News is institutionally biased are wrong."

The BBC's then-director general Tim Davie also resigned over the scandal, and was replaced by Brittin earlier this year.

The episode of Panorama spliced together two sections of a speech he delivered in 2021, shortly before the Capitol riots on 6 January.

President Trump launched a $10bn (£7.6bn) lawsuit against the BBC after the edit came to light.

The BBC apologised and said the edit had given "the mistaken impression that President Trump had made a direct call for violent action", but rejected his demand for compensation.

The case is currently scheduled to go to trial in the US in 2027.

articles.title: Niamh O'Brien: Dancer and wife of Michael Flatley dies, aged 52
articles.text:
Niamh O'Brien, a former lead performer in Lord of the Dance and the wife of Riverdance star Michael Flatley, has died at the age of 52.

Announcing her death on social media on Monday, Flatley said his "heart is broken".

"My gorgeous bride of twenty years has gone to the Lord in Heaven."

O'Brien was a renowned Irish dancer who performed the lead role of Saoirse in the Lord of the Dance shows.

Flatley described her as "the most loving mother, wife and person and our lives will never be the same without her".

The couple had a son, Michael St James, who was born in 2007.

A representative for Flatley said that O'Brien died peacefully at the Beacon Hospital in Dublin after an illness, Irish national broadcaster RTÉ reports.

"The Flatley and O'Brien families are devastated by Niamh's sudden passing and have asked that their privacy be respected as they come to terms with this heartbreaking loss," said the representative.

"They express their sincere gratitude to the doctors, nurses and staff at Beacon Hospital who cared for Niamh over the past few weeks, and to everyone who has offered their kindness and support to the family."

articles.title: Glastonbury Festival 2027: Spring ticket resale, volunteering and line-up news
articles.text:
Thousands of people were left disappointed on Sunday after tickets for Glastonbury Festival sold out in 42 minutes.

Organisers used a new booking system for the first time which entered people into a virtual waiting room. Despite having capacity for 210,000 people, demand is always much higher than supply.

But those who missed out on Sunday should not lose hope, as there are other ways to secure a ticket for the world-famous event when it returns to Worthy Farm in Somerset from 23-27 June.

Below is everything you need to know about how you can still secure a pass for the 2027 festival.

Organisers confirmed that general admission tickets sold out in 42 minutes on Sunday.

Coach package tickets, which went on sale on Thursday, sold out in less than half an hour.

Organisers confirmed last month that tickets for the weekend were at their highest price ever - £408, including a £5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of £29.50 from the last event in 2025.

In a statement on Instagram after the sale ended, organisers said: "Thank you to everyone who bought one and we're sorry to those of you who missed out on a morning where demand greatly exceeded supply.

"There will be a resale of any cancelled or returned tickets in spring 2027."

Tickets for the festival were sold exclusively by See Tickets and are strictly non-transferable.

Security will carry out thorough identification checks at all entry points on the site when the gates open to ensure validity.

Any tickets found to be bought through third parties will be cancelled and admission will be refused.

In a statement, organisers said: "If someone's claiming - whether on social media or elsewhere - they can get you Glastonbury tickets and it's not through See Tickets or directly from us, do not risk it."

They added that they are made aware of people "losing large sums of money" every year on fake tickets.

"Please do not fall victim to these scams," they said.

Although the Glastonbury Festival 2027 line-up is yet to be announced, the rumours are rife already.

Emily Eavis, co-organiser of the festival, has already confirmed that Oasis will not be performing at Worthy Farm. Liam Gallagher posted on X that "it's not happening".

Eavis also told BBC Radio 4's programme that Madonna is "definitely not" headlining either.

She did reveal that three headliners were already lined up which the team was "very excited about" - but for now, we will have to wait and find out.

The last festival in 2025 was headlined by The 1975, Neil Young and Olivia Rodrigo.

articles.title: Rachel Jupp is a bold choice for BBC News chief, says Katie Razzall
articles.text:
Rachel Jupp is a bold choice for the BBC's director of news. She is a well-regarded high flier who has impressed in her roles at Panorama, Newsnight and Channel 4 News.

She is currently the BBC's director of news documentaries and long form journalism. But she hasn't been in that role for long and hasn't spent years leading huge teams of people (BBC News' global newsroom has around 4,500 staff).

A lack of that kind of experience might have been problematic in the past. But the BBC's new director general comes from Google. Tech companies regularly appoint people who may not have the direct experience for a role but have the strategic vision and drive to make a difference. He is talking about distinctive journalism and reinvention.

Jupp's appointment signals a direction of travel both on the change that the new boss thinks is required and also on the use of technology.

BBC appoints Rachel Jupp as new director of news

Before Jupp took up her role in documentaries, she had moved to the US and was a senior member of the BBC's AI team, developing and leading the BBC's approach to artificial intelligence.

It feels significant that the former Google boss has chosen someone with that experience to run his news teams, raising questions around how AI could open up the next frontier of a modern newsroom.

But the new director of news has a lot on her plate.

She leads a news operation that is still reeling from a series of crises that eventually brought down her predecessor, Deborah Turness, as well as director general Tim Davie.

She'll have to oversee the £51m in savings that news must make (one tenth of the £500m the entire BBC must find).

Job cuts are already in train, journalists are having to reapply for their roles - and there is much more pain to come.

Staff have told me they want clear direction and an end to the salami slicing of resources. They ask what are the priorities, what are the things we do that are crucial and which are less important?

The teams she now leads will want a plan for how they can make such deep cuts without impacting the quality of what they do.

BBC News stands or falls by its on-the-ground, eyewitness journalism. Some are asking how much of that can BBC News still afford to do.

But there are also questions about whether the BBC needs to learn from its rivals by slimming down the number of stories it does and prioritizing the big hits. A streamlined BBC News.

Her challenges are both editorial and practical.

After 10 months without a permanent boss, I have picked up a sense of drift. Everybody understands - and the new DG repeats this, just as his predecessor Tim Davie did - that the BBC must go to where audiences are and where they will be in the future.

Staff at BBC News have heard this before. They want to know what it actually means in practice and how news will be reorganised.

The biggest challenge is the change in viewing habits. News has a loyal base of viewers still watching on linear channels (and who many argue should not be taken for granted in the rush to attract younger audiences online) but the direction of travel is changing fast.

There will be resistance - from viewers, from politicians, from campaign groups - as the BBC decides to move away from old formats and old technology. But it must go where audiences are and the new head of news will need a strategy to move much more deeply into a digital world.

The BBC has been doing this in a fairly piecemeal way up to now.

But Jupp will need to turbocharge it - with fewer resources and a demoralised workforce, some of whom she will need to shepherd out the door.

Brittin has talked about the bigger prize of getting the news division's trusted journalism to much larger numbers of people around the world. She has to deliver that.

She will also need to give BBC News greater editorial confidence after years of political attack and the errors of recent years.

Staff working in news would argue it was the current affairs side of the operation that previously let the organisation down. A documentary about the children of Gaza narrated by the son of a Hamas official. A documentary about Israel's assault on Gazan medical staff commissioned and then dropped by the BBC and later shown on Channel 4.

Then, of course, there are the revelations that a Panorama broadcast ahead of Donald Trump's reelection as President had spliced together two clips of the President's speech on the day of the riots on Capitol Hill - changing the editorial meaning. BBC chair Samir Shah apologised to Trump who is suing the BBC for $10bn. The court proceedings are still playing out.

Perhaps promoting Jupp - who took over the BBC News' current affairs department after the scandals - to the top of News is a signal she will grip what some have viewed as a weak spot with rigour.

Trust is one of the BBC's core values. It's listed on the back of our work passes as "the foundation of the BBC". The new boss will need to make sure that the BBC remains the place of record. An organisation that is trusted.

It's still the most trusted source of news, but there are growing numbers of people on all sides of the political spectrum who don't feel the BBC speaks for them.

Many will argue that is because people live in echo chambers online, and don't want to hear other voices.

But any loss of trust is corrosive.

articles.title: Jeremy Clarkson makes surprise appearance at Tory conference
articles.text:
Jeremy Clarkson has said it had been a "terrible" year for farming due to the hot weather, at a surprise appearance at the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham.

The former Top Gear presenter and star of Clarkson's Farm also said farmers were being "attacked" from every angle by rising costs, but he was optimistic about the future.

He was greeted by loud applause from the Tory faithful, but joked that "a lot of people have come dressed as seats, I notice, around the edges there".

In a question and answer session alongside land agent Charlie Ireland, he also criticised the economic conditions faced by business owners, asking: "Why would anybody set up a business in this country right now?"

Clarkson - who also hosts ITV's Who Wants to be a Millionaire - was introduced to the stage by the Conservative shadow environment secretary Victoria Atkins.

Asked what kind of year he had had on the farm, Clarkson said: "We worked really hard all year and we ended up with, I think I'm right in saying, three ounces of hen food.

"It was an absolute disaster on the farming side but, I mean, luckily we've got other projects going on now.

"But the farming is very, very difficult – very, very difficult at the moment."

He added: "I'm very fortunate that I do have other income streams and newspaper columns, but if you're an ordinary farmer, it's not just the weather.

"Remember, it's as Charlie was saying, the attacks come from everywhere – whether it's Iran or Ukraine or taxes or energy costs – whatever it might be, it's just relentless."

The TV presenter has long been a Conservative supporter and was involved in the campaign against the Labour government's inheritance tax plans for farmers.

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government would levy inheritance tax on family farms in the party's first budget.

But the plan was watered down last year following the farmers' campaign and pressure from some of Labour's rural MPs.

Responding to Clarkson's comments, a government source said: "We are working with farmers to strengthen domestic food production and make supply chains more resilient as we build a stronger and more profitable farming sector together."

Clarkson also joked about comments by Labour MP Jenny Riddell-Carpenter who said the Britain of country pubs and black Labradors was a "nostalgic" false memory.

He joked that he was a "socialist" because he drinks lager and has two fox red Labradors, after it was reported Riddell-Carpenter told a Labour conference fringe event she feared the far right deciding what the vision of rural areas is.

Riddell-Carpenter had said: "It'll be that warm ale, a black Labrador by your feet in a pub that doesn't exist, and with symbolism of fox hunting all around them. It'll be a very far-right nostalgic vision of Britain that we don't want to have, (that) never really existed."

articles.title: Anuv Jain: Rising Indian singer on new music and future hopes
articles.text:
Can you find success as an Indian artist, outside of the Bollywood machine, while making music that feels like you?

Well according to Anuv Jain it's possible - and you can even create something "beautiful".

The singer-songwriter's soft vocals have gained hundreds of millions of views on YouTube - not an easy feat as an independent artist in India's music scene.

BBC Newsbeat met Jain as he prepared for the final shows on the European leg of his first world tour to find out why he's taking his time and "hoping for the best".

"It's not about the numbers," Jain tells us backstage, ahead of his sold-out performance at London's Roundhouse.

But they do tell a story.

Jain is from Ludhiana in the Punjab region of India and began singing as a teenager.

His tracks have since racked up hundreds of millions of views on YouTube with their emotional storylines about relationships and heartbreak.

Jain primarily sings in Hindi, with his pieces often exploring deep emotions like love and longing.

Fans talk about feeling like his music soundtracks their lives, external and is personal to them.

His accessible style has attracted 3.9 million followers on Instagram and more than 20 million monthly listeners on Spotify.

According to Jain, the secret to his success is simple.

When writing music, he says, he imagines how someone listening in the car, going for a run or sitting alone at night would feel hearing the song.

"I just try to make a good song and something that I would like to listen to, something my mum, my sister and my wife would like to listen to," he says.

"For some reason, the taste that we have in music is gentle enough that when we put it out there, there are millions of people who are wanting to consume all of this."

Jain has attracted a sizeable fanbase without the backing of Bollywood, which has traditionally dominated the Indian music industry with opportunities and significant funding for artists.

He's one of a growing number of independent musicians offering something different to the rollicking film scores and dramatic ballads that are synonymous with the country's movie industry.

Jain describes artists like him as existing in an "alternate space".

"We release music ourselves and hope for the best," he says.

Jo Tum Mere Ho and Afsos, Jain's track with AP Dhillon, both reached number one on the Asian Music Charts, but the singer says there's no recipe to his success.

articles.title: Glastonbury Festival 2027 tickets sell out in 42 minutes
articles.text:
Tickets for Glastonbury Festival 2027 sold out in 42 minutes, organisers have said.

Thousands of people joined the online queue at 09:00 BST in the hope of securing tickets to the festival at Worthy Farm in Somerset, which returns from 23 to 27 June after a fallow year.

Organisers confirmed last month that tickets for the weekend were at their highest price ever - £408, including a £5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of £29.50 from the last event in 2025.

Headliners have yet to be announced but organiser Emily Eavis previously said the team was "very excited" and things were "coming together really well".

Glastonbury posted on Instagram shortly after 09:40 to announce that tickets had sold out, and notified those who were in the queue.

"Thank you to everyone who bought one and we're sorry to those of you who missed out on a morning where demand greatly exceeded supply," the post said.

"There will be a resale of any cancelled or returned tickets in Spring 2027."

The first round of tickets, which were for coach packages, went up for sale on Thursday and sold out in less than half an hour.

Despite the increase in cost, Zoe Scott, who has been to the festival twice, said "the price is totally worth it".

"You're getting to see thousands of acts, there's over 100 stages," she said.

"It's such a vibe at Glastonbury- everyone's so happy and free-spirited. You're just on a constant high from friends, music and the sun is usually shining".

A couple who first met at Glastonbury will also be heading to Worthy Farm next year to celebrate their 20th wedding anniversary.

Nick and Helen Nugget from Amersham met through mutual friends at the festival in 2007 and will be returning next year with the same group.

Nick told BBC Your Voice that they were "absolutely delighted" to be going back.

The couple last went to the festival in 2011- although they were successful in securing tickets in 2019, they were unable to attend due to the adoption of their daughter.

Dave in London was in several groups all trying to get tickets through their laptops and phones on Sunday morning, and was successful.

He said: "Actually it seems like it's fairer this year than it's ever been.

"All the hacks that people used to use don't seem to have the same impact, and about a quarter of the people on the groups we are on managed to get tickets."

Sarah in Dorset was surprised she also managed to get hold of some.

She said: "A mobile phone on 5G in Shaftesbury seemed to be the optimal way to get tickets. We didn't even know Shaftesbury had 5G until this morning."

Among those who were not successful were Mat Chapman and his daughter Amy.

Mat told the BBC that he used to watch the festival on TV with Amy when she was little, promising to take her when she was five years old as "she always wanted to have her own flag that you could see on the telly".

Mat had hoped that after 20 years of trying, he would be able to beat the queue this year, on Amy's 26th birthday. Unfortunately he only ever moved from "two bar hell to three bar purgatory".

"There's always next year. We'll fly the flag there one day."

This year's Glastonbury tickets have breached the £400 mark for the first time.

Tickets have increased over the years, from £185 in 2010 to £408 for the upcoming 2027 line-up.

Most price rises have come since the pandemic, with tickets climbing from £318 in 2019 to a peak of £408 in 2027.

But unlike recent years, much of the 2010s saw relatively steady price hikes.

Any tickets from today's sale that are not paid for in full by the early April 2027 deadline will be put back into an official resale pool, festival organisers said.

The exact date for this is yet to be announced, but in previous years it has been in late April.

articles.title: Matthew Rhys wins Best Actor for The Beast in Me at Bafta Cymru
articles.text:
Matthew Rhys has continued his fine form this awards season after being announced as the Best Actor at the Bafta Cymru Awards ceremony.

The actor made history last month when he became the first person to win two lead acting prizes in one night at the Emmy's.

Presenter Carol Vorderman said she was "humbled and excited" to receive an award for outstanding contribution, while Lauren Evans took home an award for her contribution to the film I Swear.

Lee Walters, Bafta Cymru chair, congratulated the nominees last month, and said "each is a testament to the creativity, skill and dedication of the people working across Wales' screen industries, both in front of and behind the camera".

Rhys was presented with the award for his performance in The Beast in Me, earning him his second Bafta Cymru, 29 years after his first for his role in the Welsh-language film Bydd yn Wro, or Be Brave.

Gabrielle Creevy won her second Best Actress award and Y Crwydryn took home the Single Documentary award, with Rhys Edwards winning Director Factual for the same show.

Mari Grug won her first Bafta Cymru award for presenter in Mari Grug: Un Dydd Ar y Tro.

Elsewhere, Y Golau: Dwr won two awards and Matthew Barry won Best Writer for The Guest.

Amour a Mynydd won the Entertainment Programme award and Stori'r Iaith received the Factual Series award.

Burton won the Feature/Television Film award and the Short Film award was won by Gofod Ymennydd - Brain Space and the Children's Programme went to Itopia.

In total, 17 awards were presented across the evening, which took place at the ICC Wales, in Newport, as well as two Bafta Outstanding Contribution awards.
